UX research Visual Identity Website Design
Aligning Teams, Audiences, and Priorities Into a Unified Experience

Key audiences lacked clear pathways to the information they needed. The site contained valuable content, but the information architecture did not prioritize prospective clients and potential new employees

The North American site felt disconnected from a strong global brand. The NA site had developed its own look and feel rather than leveraging Obayashi’s established global identity, making the relationship unclear.

Internal priorities had not been translated into a clear external hierarchy HR, Engineering, Safety, Operations, and leadership each had different priorities for the site. The challenge was determining which messages mattered most to the business and its audiences.

The digital experience did not reflect the sophistication of the work Obayashi delivers large-scale projects requiring precision, coordination, and technical expertise. A fragmented digital experience risked communicating the opposite.
Obayashi North America had a website, but it lacked a clear digital story.
Designing Around Projects,  People, and Expertise

I compared Obayashi’s website with competitors to assess how they presented their capabilities, projects, culture, and brand. This revealed opportunities to improve navigation, visual storytelling, project content, and audience pathways, establishing a benchmark for the redesign.

I translated the research findings into a clearer site structure, making projects easier to discover and giving their scale, technical complexity, and impact more visibility. Early sketches informed reusable page layouts and a consistent visual system that strengthened Obayashi’s North American identity across the site.
Storyboard Whiteboard in Dark Green Pastel Green Beige Simple and Minimal Style 1

I interviewed 17 internal stakeholders across Engineering, HR, Executive Leadership, Safety, Operations, and IT to understand what each department needed the website to communicate. These interviews captured internal priorities and perceptions of audience needs.

Different priorities pointed to two central needs: demonstrating Obayashi’s capabilities to prospective clients and helping candidates understand the employee experience. I organized technical expertise around markets and relevant North American projects, while giving culture, benefits, and career growth a dedicated recruiting pathway.

Across departments, recurring themes of trust, collaboration, mentorship, growth, and community also emerged. These themes informed the brand story and employee storytelling, connecting the company’s capabilities with the people behind its work.
I created a storyboard that brought recurring themes to life through employee perspectives, project footage, company culture, and community involvement.
“The website is often the first impression people have of Obayashi. It should reflect the scale of our work and the people behind it.”
I mapped the findings into priorities for content, navigation, visual design, and measurement to guide the  website strategy and redesign.
The themes became a visual language. I selected key themes to bring to life through authentic moments across the organization.
Where the Existing Experience Fell Short
I audited Obayashi’s existing website to identify gaps in navigation, content, and visual hierarchy that could make it harder for visitors to find what they needed. 4 key insights emerged:
Prospective clients were key to new business, but the site relied on a basic contact page, with no inquiry forms or contextual contact links.
North American projects were difficult to find
Projects were the content users most wanted to see, yet the Work page redirected them to a visually inconsistent global site where North American projects were buried.
Sparse project descriptions made it difficult for prospective clients to assess each project’s scale, key partners, technical complexity, and impact.
Sparse content on culture, benefits, and career growth made it difficult for candidates to picture what working at Obayashi would be like.

Re-center navigation around North American work Create clear explanations of global structure Rebuild case studies to reflect real project depth Introduce employee storytelling for recruiting Reduce external redirects to maintain continuity
Define North America’s role within the global brand.
Bring employees, culture, and community into the story.
Center the needs of prospective clients and candidates.
Make projects and capabilities easier to find.

Established a clear North American identity Made projects discoverable and credible Improved navigation across multiple audiences Strengthened alignment between internal teams and external messaging  The redesign was presented to leadership and is currently in final implementation.
Establish a self-contained North American site, eliminating redirects to the Tokyo site that disrupted user journeys, blurred regional identity, and made the North American site feel secondary.

Information architecture creates organizational clarity. Organizing the site meant clarifying how teams, services, and projects fit into one North American identity.  Business goals need to guide content priorities. Balancing departmental requests taught me to prioritize paths for prospective clients and job candidates to support business growth and recruitment, while keeping essential content like safety accessible.  Small structural decisions can have big impact. Removing redirects to the Tokyo site reduced navigation friction and clarified Obayashi’s North American presence.
Project pages that expose scope, partners,  technical challenges, and impact.
Technology page makes Obayashi’s expertise  easier to explore,
The Careers page brings the employee experience to life through photos, interviews,  testimonials, and a “Why Obayashi” section.
Rail & Transit page highlights key projects  within the sector.
